summary: Poses open questions about path-aware networking, where endpoints can see properties of available paths and choose among them. Some of this exists within single domains already, while a fully path-aware internetwork would extend it across layers and the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Path-aware networking would let the programs at each end of a connection see what the route between them looks like, for example its delay or its loss, and pick among the available routes. Today's Internet hides that: the network chooses the path and the endpoints cannot check its properties. This RFC is a list of eight open questions that would have to be answered before such an architecture could be built.

questions: open questions in path selection by endpoints
how do endpoints discover network paths
why should endpoints choose their own paths
subtitle: Eight open research questions about letting endpoints see and choose the paths their traffic takes.

tldr.problem: In today's Internet the network picks the path for a flow and gives the endpoints no way to check what that path is like, so an application cannot ask for a better one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9217 defines path-aware networking as endpoint discovery of path properties and endpoint reaction to them, then poses eight questions covering the vocabulary of path properties, their distribution and trust, path selection, interfaces between layers, transport-layer effects, endpoints, operations and deployment.
tldr.outcome: The document answers none of the questions. It is published with the rough consensus of the Path Aware Networking Research Group as a research agenda, and it has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9217 is an Informational document published in March 2022 with the rough consensus of the Path Aware Networking Research Group. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It poses questions and proposes no answers, so the eight questions it lists remain research topics.

sections.title: What Path-Aware Networking Would Change
sections.content:
In the current Internet architecture the network layer provides a best-effort service to the endpoints using it, with no verifiability of the properties of the path between them. Some network-layer technologies attempt better-than-best-effort delivery, but their interfaces are generally administrative rather than exposed to endpoints, as with Path Computation Element (PCE) and Software-Defined Wide Area Network approaches, and they are often restricted to a single administrative domain. In this architecture an application can assume that a packet with a given destination address will eventually be forwarded toward that destination, and little else. A transport protocol such as TCP can add reliability over that service and a protocol above the network layer, such as TLS, can authenticate the remote endpoint, but little explicit information about the path reaches the endpoints, and assumptions made about that path often do not hold, with serious consequences as in BGP hijacking attacks.

In a path-aware internetworking architecture, endpoints can select or influence the paths through the network used by a given packet or flow. The network and transport layers explicitly expose information about the available paths to the endpoints and to the applications running on them. The Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) protocol can be seen as an example of a path-awareness approach implemented in transport-layer terms on the present Internet protocol stack. Path selection gives applications and users explicit visibility and control of network treatment. Path control at the flow and subflow level enables the design of new transport protocols that can use multipath connectivity across disjoint paths, even over a single physical interface, and when exposed to applications or to end users through a configuration interface it allows constraints to be set on the paths traffic should traverse, for instance to confound passive surveillance in the network core.

The document notes that path awareness already exists in many Internet-connected networks within single domains: much of the practice of network engineering with encapsulation at layer 3 assigns traffic at tunnel endpoints to a given path inside the network. Path-aware internetworking seeks to extend that awareness across domain boundaries without resorting to overlays, except as a transition technology.

Two definitions follow. Path-aware networking describes endpoint discovery of the properties of paths used for communication across an internetwork, and endpoint reaction to those properties that affects routing or data transfer. A path-aware internetwork is one in which endpoint discovery of path properties and endpoint selection of paths are explicitly supported, regardless of the specific design of the protocol features that enable this. A path is abstractly defined as a sequence of adjacent path elements over which a packet can be transmitted, where the definition of a path element is technology dependent; since the document poses questions rather than answers them, it assumes that this definition will be refined as part of the answer to the first two questions.
sections.plainLanguage: Today an application can trust only that its packets will head in the right general direction. It cannot find out that the path is slow, that it passes through a place it did not want to be, or that it has been tampered with. Path-aware networking means making that information visible to the two ends of the connection and letting them act on it. Much of this already happens inside single networks; the document is about carrying it across network boundaries.

sections.title: A Vocabulary of Path Properties
sections.content:
The first question is how paths and path properties are defined and represented. For information about paths to reach an endpoint, and for the endpoint to use it, there has to be a common vocabulary for paths through an internetwork and for the properties of those paths. Its elements could include terminology for the components of a path, properties defined for those components, for the entire path, or for subpaths of a path. The properties may be relatively static, such as the presence of a given node or service function on the path, or relatively dynamic, such as the current values of metrics like loss and latency.

The vocabulary and its representation have to be designed carefully, because their design affects the expressiveness, scalability and security of the resulting architecture. A system that exposes node-level information for the topology of each network would maximize the information about the individual components of the path at the endpoints, at the cost of making internal network topology universally public, which may conflict with the business goals of each network's operator. Properties tied to individual components of a path may also change frequently and become outdated quickly. Aggregating the properties of individual components to distill end-to-end properties for the whole path is not trivial.
sections.plainLanguage: The first thing to settle is the words themselves: what can be said about a path, and how it is written down. The trade-off is between telling the endpoints everything, which reveals each network's internal layout, and saying very little, which leaves the endpoint unable to reason about the path it is on.

sections.title: Getting Path Properties to the Endpoints
sections.content:
The second question is how endpoints and applications get access to accurate, useful and trustworthy path properties. Once endpoints and networks share a vocabulary, the network needs some method for distributing the path properties to the endpoints. Whatever the method, the endpoints need a way to authenticate the properties, so that they can determine that the properties originated from and pertain to the path they claim to describe.

The choices affect scalability. The space of distribution methods includes in band versus out of band, push versus pull versus publish-subscribe, and similar dimensions. There are also timing problems, especially with dynamic properties: the measurement or elicitation of a dynamic property may be outdated by the time the information reaches the endpoints, and the interaction between measurement delay and dissemination delay may behave badly for unlucky points in the parameter space.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing the words is not enough. The properties have to reach the endpoints, and the endpoints have to be able to check that the numbers they received really describe the path they are on. The document notes that properties like delay change quickly, so a measurement can be stale before it is even delivered.

sections.title: Supporting Path Selection
sections.content:
The third question is how endpoints can select paths for their traffic in a way that can be trusted by the network, the endpoints and the applications using them. Access to trustworthy path properties is only half the challenge; endpoints must be able to use that information to select paths for specific traffic they send.

As with dissemination, the choices made in path-selection methods affect the trade-off between scalability and expressiveness. One key choice is between in-band and out-of-band control of path selection. Another is the granularity of path selection, whether per packet, per flow or per larger aggregate, which has a large impact on the same trade-off. Path selection must also be trustworthy, so that the result of a selection at an endpoint is predictable, and any path-selection mechanism should aim to provide an outcome that is not worse than using a single path or selecting paths at random.

Path selection may be expressed in terms of the properties of the path or in terms of the identity of elements of the path. In the latter case a path may be identified at any of several layers, such as a routing domain identifier, a network-layer address, or a higher-layer identifier or name, and care must be taken to present semantically useful information to whoever is deciding which path to trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Given good information, the endpoint still has to pick. The design choices are about how much freedom it gets: whether the choice is made in the packet flow or out of band, and whether it applies to every packet, to each flow, or to a larger group of traffic. The endpoint also has to be able to predict what the network will do with its choice.

sections.title: Interfaces, Transport Layers and Endpoints
sections.content:
The fourth question is how interfaces among the network, transport and application layers can support the use of path awareness. For applications to make effective use of a path-aware architecture, the control interfaces presented by the network and transport layers must expose path properties to the application in a useful way and offer a useful set of paths to choose from. Path selection must be possible based on the preferences and policies of the application developer and of end users alike, and the interfaces must support multiple levels of granularity: most application requirements can be met by expressing path-selection policies in terms of path properties, while some applications need finer-grained per-path control. The interfaces also need to support incremental development and deployment, and to provide sensible defaults, to avoid hindering adoption.

The fifth question is how transport-layer and higher-layer protocols should be redesigned to work most effectively over a path-aware networking layer. In the current Internet the assumption that all traffic of a given flow receives the same network treatment and traverses the same path, or equivalent paths, often holds. In a path-aware network that assumption is more easily violated, which has implications for the design of protocols above such a layer. One advantage of multipath communication is that a flow can be sprayed along multiple paths to confound attempts to collect data or metadata for pervasive surveillance. Those benefits are reduced if upper-layer protocols use linkable identifiers on packets belonging to the same flow across different paths. Clients may mitigate linkability by choosing not to reuse cleartext connection identifiers such as TLS session IDs or tickets on separate paths, but the strategies required for effective privacy in a path-aware Internet are only possible if higher-layer protocols such as TLS let clients obtain unlinkable identifiers.

The sixth question asks how path awareness, in terms of vocabulary and interfaces, differs when applied to tunnel and overlay endpoints. The vision so far assumes that path properties are disseminated to endpoints on which applications are running, such as terminals with user agents and servers. Incremental deployment may instead require a path-aware network core to interconnect islands of legacy protocol networks, and in those cases the gateways, not the application endpoints, receive path properties and make path selections for that traffic. The interfaces a gateway provides are necessarily different from those a path-aware networking layer provides to its transport and application layers, and the path property information the gateway needs and makes available may also differ.
sections.plainLanguage: The layers have to talk to each other about paths. The network layer has to tell the transport layer what is available, and the transport layer has to tell the application in a form the application can use. There is one more case: during a gradual transition, a path-aware core may join up islands of older networks, and there the gateways, not the applications, are the ones making the choices.

sections.title: Operating and Deploying a Path-Aware Network
sections.content:
The seventh question is how a path-aware network within a path-aware internetwork can be effectively operated, given control inputs from network administrators, application designers and end users. The operations model of the current Internet assumes that traffic flows are controlled by the decisions and policies of network operators as expressed in interdomain and intradomain routing protocols. In a network that offers path selection to endpoints, that assumption no longer holds, because endpoints may react to path properties by selecting alternate paths. Competing control inputs from path-aware endpoints and from the routing control plane may lead to harder traffic engineering or non-convergent forwarding, especially when the endpoints' and the operators' idea of the best path diverges. Explicit path selection can specify outbound paths, while BGP policies are expressed in terms of inbound traffic.

A concept for path-aware network operations needs clear methods for resolving apparent, if not actual, conflicts of intent between the operator and the path selection at an endpoint, and a set of safety principles so that increasing path control does not reduce connectivity. One such principle could be that the existence of at least one path between two endpoints guarantees the selection of at least one path between those endpoints.

The eighth question is how the incentives of network operators and end users can be aligned to realize the vision, and how the transition from current, path-oblivious operation to path-aware operation can be managed. The vision is written from the point of view of the benefits accruing at endpoints, to designers of transport protocols and applications and to the end users of those applications, but it requires action inside the interconnected networks offering path-aware connectivity, and any path-aware architecture will require network operators to give up some control of their networks to endpoint-driven control inputs. The question of apparent versus actual conflicts of intent arises again: some network operation requirements may appear essential but be accidents of the interfaces provided by current routing and management protocols. The widespread use of the TCP wire image in network monitoring for DDoS prevention, the document notes, appears to conflict with the deployment of encrypted transports only because path signaling has been implicit in past transport protocols. The incentives for operators and equipment vendors need to be made clear in terms of a plan to transition an internetwork to path-aware operation, one network and facility at a time, and that plan has to take into account that the dynamics early in the transition, when few endpoints and flows use path selection, differ from those later on. Data security and information management also have to be addressed, in a network that explicitly radiates more information about its deployment and configuration and implicitly radiates information about endpoint configuration and preference through path selection.

On security and privacy, the document poses questions whose answers belong to future research, and notes that the security considerations for those answers would be included in the RFCs that eventually describe them. Of the eight questions, the ones on discovery and trustworthiness are the most security-relevant.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting endpoints choose paths changes who is in charge. Network operators set routing policy; endpoints may now pick paths that operators did not intend, which can make traffic engineering harder. The document asks how that conflict is resolved and how operators and users can be given a reason to move over, one network at a time.
